title: County Monaghan bomb: Law student charged over device in car
description: A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.Isobella Perrie Sullivan,
body: A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Abbeylands Park in Clane, County Kildare, was charged with the possession of explosives.It was alleged she was driving the car which was intercepted by gardaí (Irish police) near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday.A defence solicitor told the court his client had been asked to take a bag to Northern Ireland and had not been aware what was in it.Earlier on Friday, gardaí (Irish police) told reporters their interception was part of an operation targeting dissident republican activity. The accused, who was arrested on Wednesday, was brought before a special sitting of Trim District Court in County Meath on Friday evening.A member of the Garda Special Detective Unit told the court the car she was driving was stopped by officers on N2 at Aclint, south of Carrickmacross.

schema.headline: County Monaghan bomb: Law student charged over device in car

title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
description: It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.
body: It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.There should be scope for a better deal for the UK, but it raises an interesting question about whether the government will pursue an EU-style ban. This is widely seen as a backdoor way to target China, in particular for conditions in its Xinjiang province.Last October, external the government said it "remained firmly opposed to the use of state-imposed forced labour", but that it was "considering how best to reflect this position," citing "operational and legal complexities".Since then, the UK has welcomed imports of Chinese cars, and is exploring a services trade deal with the country. The relationship with China has been a balancing act for the government.This is also one of the global stories of the tariff wars. As the US repeatedly changes its rationale for tariffs, the rest of the world is focused on trading with each other. For example, Canada increased its trade with the rest of the world by more than it lost from the US.China's total dollar trade with the US is flat in the first half of this year versus last year. Across the world it is up 21%, including 14% with the EU, 11% with the UK, and 24% with Africa.There could be pressure now to legislate for a formal ban on forced labour products. Successive governments have opted for a lighter voluntary due diligence regime.Will the US force a change in the UK and elsewhere, and what might it offer in return?Or the UK may opt to keep its precarious geopolitical position by sticking to its existing deals in medicines, metals and cars.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating

title: Trump vows to investigate EU over fining of US tech companies
description: Donald Trump says the US will launch an investigation into the European Union and threatened a fresh tariff over fines handed to some of the biggest A
body: Donald Trump says the US will launch an investigation into the European Union and threatened a fresh tariff over fines handed to some of the biggest American tech companies. It comes days after the European Commission fined Google €890m ($1bn) for operating in a way that squeezed out competitors to its services.In a post to Truth Social, which Trump owns, the US president said the EU would pay a "very big price" over how it had treated Google, along with other major US tech companies Apple, Meta, and Amazon, which have also been investigated."The United States of America is not a "PIGGYBANK" for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!" he wrote.Trump said any fines should be "entirely reversed" and that he was initiating a trade investigation of the EU while considering "a substantial TARIFF".He added that the US would "immediately initiate a 301 investigation" over European regulators' alleged practice of "robbing American companies and, in turn, the American taxpayer". Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, external gives The Office of the United States Trade Representative the power to react and investigate trade practices believed to be unfair. The second Trump Administration has launched several such investigations, external since last year.The tariff threat comes just one day after Trump announced new tariffs on 60 trading partners, including the EU, UK and China, of between 10% and 12.5%. Trump also last month threatened a 100% import tariff on any European country that introduces a digital services tax on American technology giants, despite many such nations already doing so, external for years.Major tech companies, including Google, Meta, Apple, and Amazon, have donated millions of dollars to funds behind Trump's campaign and presidency.  José Castañeda, a spokesman for Google, told the BBC the company had "worked hard to comply" with Europe's Digital Markets Act but had "expressed our concerns about the impact of recent EC decisions"."We appreciate the engagement by the administration and US government," Castañeda added.In addition to the recent fine against Google, Trump claimed in his post that Apple had received EU fines of $15bn, Meta fines of $3bn, and Amazon fines of $2.5bn. Representatives of Meta, Apple and Amazon, as well as the European Commission, have been contacted for comment.It was not clear where the figures cited by Trump come from. Shortly before Trump was elected president in 2024, he said Tim Cook, Apple's chief executive, had called him directly to complain about fines the company had received from European regulators.The call came not long after Apple lost a long-running dispute over unpaid taxes.Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has been fined several times by EU regulators, including for violations of user privacy and competition laws, external. It is also facing new fines over purportedly "addictive" features of its apps. Meta last year said the EU was "attempting to handicap successful American businesses".Amazon, however, appears to have been investigated at times by the European Commission, but avoided major fines. The company in 2022 reached an agreement with regulators to change some of its practices in Europe.

schema.headline: Trump vows to investigate EU over fining of US tech companies

title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?
description: ByBen ChuBBC Verify and Tom EdgingtonBBC VerifyAndy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 N
body: ByBen ChuBBC Verify and Tom EdgingtonBBC VerifyAndy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about £1.5bn. Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line.End rough sleeping in EnglandCost: £340m over five years, fundedIn his speech outside Downing Street , externalon Monday, Burnham said his "first instruction" would be "to end rough sleeping in our country".The most recent official data , externalsuggests that there were around 4,800 people sleeping rough on a single night in England in 2025, up from 1,800 in 2010.The government announced that Burnham's "instruction" would be delivered by £340m of spending, which it said would support at least 3,000 people over a five year period.It said this money would come from existing "uncommitted" budgets in the housing department.This means that the funding has been made available by the Treasury to the department but had not yet been assigned to a specific project.VAT cut from electricity billsCost: £850m, unfundedOn Tuesday morning the Treasury announced that it would cut, external VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, knocking an estimated £45 from the typical household's annual bill from the autumn.It said this would cost £850m in 2026-27 - to be funded by scrapping the previous government's digital ID scheme, which had been estimated to cost £1.8bn over the next three years.However, the Office for Budget Responsibility, the official spending watchdog, made clear in the last budget that the digital ID scheme was itself "unfunded" , externalat that stage.That implies that while scrapping the digital ID scheme will reduce a spending pressure on the government it will not, in itself, pay for the VAT cut.That tax cut will have to be funded in the next budget, either by tax rises or specific spending cuts elsewhere.£2 cap on bus faresCost: £500m, fundedOn Wednesday, the government announced it would reduce the cap on bus fares, external in England from £3 to £2 from 1 January 2027, though this does not include London.It estimated this cap would cost the Department for Transport more than £500m.It said most of this would be found by replacing grants for international climate projects with loans. This would save the government money because the loans would be expected to be paid back in full, plus interest, freeing up funds to pay for the bus cap policy.But there are still uncertainties with this approach, said Max Warner from the Institute for Fiscal Studies."It's not clear how much we would expect to be paid back nor what the interest rates will be," he said.Cut in business rates for pubsCost: £100m, fundedOn Thursday the government announced it would cut business rates for pubs, external, clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from April 2027, saving a typical pub £1,100.It estimated that this tax cut would cost the Treasury around £100m a year.The government claimed it would be "fully funded" but did not provide details, beyond stating that part of the cost would be met by "reviewing reliefs for businesses that do not make a positive contribution to local communities, such as vape shops". It did not state what other kinds of businesses would fall into this category.Image source, Getty ImagesThe Starmer government had already announced a business rates support package, external for pubs in England in January, with a 15% cut applying in the current financial year of 2026-27 and a real-terms freeze in their rates for the subsequent two years.At that time officials estimated that package would cost £80m in its first year, and the cost in the subsequent two years would be calculated in due course by the Office for Budget Responsibility.The latest business support for pubs from the Burnham government will come on top of that earlier support - so the Treasury will have to provide an official costing for the overall package announced since January in the Autumn budget.No 10 NorthCost: Downing Street says no additional cost to taxpayers, fundedBurnham ended his first week as PM by working out of the new No 10 North, external, based at Heron House in Manchester's city centre, which he claimed will be the "situation room for making Britain better".He's expected to work from there each week, with other ministers including Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster Louise Haigh, who is overseeing the department as part of her role, also working there on a regular basis.  Up to 300 civil servants are expected to join the operation by the end of the next year, but Downing Streets insists it will cost taxpayers no extra money."The running of No 10 North will be covered by existing Cabinet Office budgets. There is no additional cost to taxpayers", Burnham's spokesman told reporters earlier this week.How does it all add up?These pledges add up to about £1.5bn. That might sound like a lot, but they are small commitments relative to overall government spending, which is projected to be around £1.4 trillion (£1,400bn) this year - making it about 0.1% of total public spending.The bigger question is whether Burnham is likely to follow through with some of the more expensive policies he's previously signalled, including reforming social care or expanding council house building.Burnham earlier this week indicated he could raise the income tax personal allowance, which the Institute for Fiscal Studies has estimated could end up costing £8.5-9bn but the idea of this happening imminently was downplayed within days.  Chancellor John Healey is likely to want to take defence spending from 2.7% to 3% of GDP by 2030, given he resigned as Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the Treasury's failure to commit the money to do that. But that would cost an additional £9bn a year in today's money.Burnham has also promised the "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period". While the details are unclear, estimates from the Centre for Cities think tanks , externalsuggest that to match the English council house building rates of the 1950s to the 1970s would require another £13bn a year in public subsidy.Policies on this scale, which could run into several billions, would likely need to be set out in future budgets and spending reviews, alongside detailed plans about how they would be paid for.However, Burnham has said he will stick to the government's existing fiscal rules - not borrowing for day-to-day spending and having debt fall as a share of the economy by the end of the Parliament.That means any major new spending commitments would likely require difficult choices: such as raising taxes or cutting spending elsewhere.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?

title: Man tells of attempt to save drowning girl and mum at West Mersea
description: A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.Craig Bowe, 42, ba
body: A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.Craig Bowe, 42, battled the incoming tide at West Mersea, near Colchester, three times after hearing screams on Wednesday evening.The kitchen fitter, who was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday, managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat.Despite his efforts, the pair - aged 41 and 15 - died in the desperate attempt to bring the boy to shore.The boy, who became stranded during a family day out from Barking, east London, was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.Three others were taken by ambulance to another hospital after the incident unfolded at about 17:35 BST.Bowe, from Northaw, sprang into action after hearing a man screaming in the water and seeing bodies floating."When I got there, the first two people I saw were actually face down, so [it was] more serious than I initially thought," he told the BBC.Bowe pulled Shally Rahman to shore where bystanders began administering CPR. He then dashed back out to sea to rescue her daughter.Having done so, he then returned to the water to help load the seven-year-old boy and another child, who were about 150 yards (137m) out at sea, onto a lifeboat."I helped sort of shoo him onto the boat, because he was face down too... but the seven-year-old was not in a good way," said Bowe, who was helped by an unnamed man."The waves were hitting me in the face. The current was definitely stronger."

schema.headline: Man tells of attempt to save drowning girl and mum at West Mersea

title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
description: "We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing s
body: "We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen, external" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that – he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead – both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him. He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.She teased the new prime minister over his informal style – he "seems like a nice guy…I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin."Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.Firstly, on the domestic front – his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options – which criminals to free first.Secondly, on the international front – after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again.Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe. Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister? Given the intended long term home of No 10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032, this is a live question.And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all – that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model". It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one – where is your mandate for doing this?The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction. It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.In other words, whether he is popular enough.Let's see.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham

title: First person gets new experimental vaccine for Bundibugyo species of Ebola
description: Prof Teresa Lambe, who led the Ebola vaccine team at the University of Oxford, said they had been able to create it so quickly because of the backgrou
body: Prof Teresa Lambe, who led the Ebola vaccine team at the University of Oxford, said they had been able to create it so quickly because of the background of decades of research.​​She explained how they would confirm that the vaccine was effective at protecting people. It cannot give anyone Ebola. ​​"We will not be giving anybody Ebola in this trial or any trial.  "The aim of the phase one clinical study is to look for the safety of the vaccine, and also to see if we're getting a strong immune response that could be protective against the Bundibugyo species of Ebola."​​There are four vaccines in development against the Bundibugyo species which has triggered the outbreak, but this is the first to enter human trials.​​There is a licensed vaccine against the Zaire species of Ebola, but it does not work against Bundibugyo.​​The Oxford team say a second small Ebola vaccine trial is due to begin soon in Uganda, followed by a bigger study, looking at efficacy, in DR Congo.​​The Serum Institute in India has already manufactured 600,000 doses of the Oxford Ebola vaccine, ready to be used if the trials are successful.​​To date there have been more than 2,500 confirmed cases of Ebola in DR Congo, including just over 1,000 deaths.

schema.headline: First person gets new experimental vaccine for Bundibugyo species of Ebola

title: Heatwave anxiety can make you feel 'incredibly helpless' - here's how to manage it
description: At the peak of the June heatwave, the warmest June on record in England, all Tavia Watts could think about was how hot it was in her two- and five-yea
body: At the peak of the June heatwave, the warmest June on record in England, all Tavia Watts could think about was how hot it was in her two- and five-year-old's bedroom - above 30C in some cases."During the heatwave, I've got a high level of anxiety all the time and I'm pretty much useless," she told the BBC. "I've had to leave bedtime when my husband reads [my kids] stories to have a little cry and to calm down, because it's just too hot in their room and I'm afraid for them."Feeling "incredibly helpless", the 36-year-old posted a short reel to her hundreds of followers on Instagram, in which she voiced her inner anxieties. To her surprise, it got more than 18,000 likes and 1,700 reposts.In the video Tavia, a stay-at-home mum living in Cheltenham, says the heat "feels like the world is literally ending", she's "terrified for [her] children's lives", and that she "wants to scream at the people not taking this seriously".Watts is not alone. A 2022 study from the University of Bath estimates that about 4.6% of people in the UK have climate anxiety, which is recognised as a form of mental distress by professional bodies and the NHS. Young people and women are among the groups most at risk, according to a study published in 2025."Anticipatory anxiety", related to heatwaves in particular, has become more common, say psychologists Dr Caroline Hickman from the University of Bath and Dr Emma Lawrance from the University of Oxford."Once people have been through a traumatic event like a flood or a heatwave, they anticipate the next one," Hickman, who offers therapy to individuals experiencing climate anxiety, told the BBC.In the UK, "now we're getting the repeat, repeat, repeat [heatwaves]. It triggers that sense that 'I can't be safe in the world, and the world can't be trusted'," she added.In June's heatwave, Hickman said she "had people saying they're going to kill themselves, I've had people saying they're going to terminate pregnancies, I've had people saying that they want to sell their houses and move somewhere cooler".Watts said that her video "clearly struck a chord with people" - including therapists posting comments about coping mechanisms - and that she wanted to help others deal with climate anxiety."It can go one of two ways. You can either just fall into doomism and think, 'What is the point?'" she said."Or you can try to do something. I sign petitions during a heatwave; I organise climate community events; I run a free children's clothes swap shop. During the last heatwave, I finally became vegetarian, because then I can tell my kids at least I tried."Lawrance had some recommendations on how to cope with climate anxiety:Talk to others: There's often "a huge perception gap between how concerned people are about climate change, and how much they think other people care", said Lawrance - meaning you might wrongly assume that you're in the minority, or even that you're alone."Make space to be kind to yourself, to tend to those emotions and know that it's coming from a place of care for the world," she added.Find a community: Lawrance recommended finding a strong social network who care about the same things, and taking positive action together. Whether it's planting a garden in your school or putting solar panels on the roof of your business, action can not only help you channel your anxiety into something positive, but can help alleviate the symptoms of anxiety too.Lawrance cited the Climate Psychology Alliance in the UK for further support, as well as groups like the Resilience Project, the Climate Cares Centre, and the Climate Majority Project.Keep yourself cool: Your physical health also affects your mental health, and being hot can also make your anxiety and mood worse, Lawrance said - so she recommended making sure to keep yourself physically cool in extreme heat."Having a cool shower, putting a cold washer on your neck, making sure you're hydrated - all of those things will help physiologically as well," she said. "There's a lot we can do - we're not powerless."

schema.headline: Heatwave anxiety can make you feel 'incredibly helpless' - here's how to manage it

title: Slapping therapist jailed over death 'released early'
description: An alternative healer jailed over the death of a woman at one of his workshops has been released from prison just 18 months into a 10-year sentence, i
body: An alternative healer jailed over the death of a woman at one of his workshops has been released from prison just 18 months into a 10-year sentence, it is understood.Hongchi Xiao, 63, from California, was convicted and sentenced in 2024 for the manslaughter by gross negligence of 71-year-old Danielle Carr-Gomm in 2016. Carr-Gomm, who was diabetic, died while taking part in a therapy event in Wiltshire, which involved people being slapped or slapping themselves repeatedly.On Friday, during a Court of Appeal hearing where an application to overturn his conviction was quashed, it emerged Xiao had been returned to the US and was believed to no longer be in custody. In his judgment, Lord Justice Dingemans said it seemed Xiao had been returned to the US on 2 July through the Early Removal Scheme.This enables eligible foreign national offenders to be deported from the UK once they have served the minimum required proportion of their sentence.However, he added: "Other information suggests he was deported on 30 June 2026. It seems that Mr Xiao is not in custody in the USA."A government spokesperson said: "Hongchi Xiao's crimes were terrible, and our thoughts remain with his victims."This government is deporting foreign national offenders at pace, with more than 5,000 deported last year, and Hongchi Xiao is prohibited from ever returning to the UK."They added if Xiao were to return to the UK, he will be liable to serve the rest of his sentence from the point he was deported.In a judgment, he also said: "As it is, we do not consider that the judge's comments about the waiver rendered the trial unfair or the verdict unsafe."This is because the judge was simply pointing out that the waiver did not reflect the reality of the relationship between Ms Carr-Gomm and Mr Xiao."He said Mr Justice Bright did misdirect the jury about the waiver, but only on it being potentially "decisive" if it were a civil trial instead of a criminal one.However, Lord Justice Dingemans said that "a legally correct direction from the judge" would have "created more difficulties for Mr Xiao because it would have made plain that Mr Xiao was seeking to rely on a waiver that had no legal effect".He added: "For the detailed reasons set out above, we dismiss the appeal against conviction."The trial at Winchester Crown Court heard Carr-Gomm, who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in 1999, was "howling in pain" and "frothing at the mouth" as she became seriously ill before she died on the fourth day of the workshop.Jurors were told she had sought alternatives to her insulin medication because of her vegetarianism and fear of needles.The court heard she had provided a testimonial for Xiao, describing him as a "messenger sent by God" who was "starting a revolution to put the power back in the hands of the people to cure themselves and to change the whole system of health care".She joined the Paida Lajin workshop, which means "slap and stretch", in October 2016, having attended another in Bulgaria a few months earlier where she also stopped her insulin medication and became seriously ill before recovering.The court heard Xiao had said "well done" to Carr-Gomm after she told the participants in Wiltshire that she had stopped taking her insulin at the week-long retreat, and she again became seriously ill.Xiao had been extradited from Australia for the trial into Carr-Gomm's death. He had previously been prosecuted there after a six-year-old boy also died when his parents withdrew his insulin medication after attending Xiao's workshop in Sydney.

schema.headline: Slapping therapist jailed over death 'released early'

title: Uganda's Ghetto Kids: Dancing with Shakira and Burna Boy at the World Cup 'very, very, very, very, very good'
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The children say joining Shakira and Burna Boy on stage was a dream come trueByNatasha Booty and BBC World Se
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The children say joining Shakira and Burna Boy on stage was a dream come trueByNatasha Booty and BBC World ServiceUgandan dance group the Ghetto Kids are celebrating another milestone after appearing at the football World Cup final half-time show on Sunday - a life-changing experience summed up by 10-year-old Sierra as "very, very, very, very, very good".Despite critics bemoaning the addition of a Superbowl-style show, external to the beautiful game's biggest event, the children's performance alongside global stars Burna Boy and Shakira was viewed by many millions around the world.Speaking to the BBC's Newsday programme, members of the dance troupe and their manager say that rising from humble beginnings in Uganda's capital, Kampala, then finding fame while balancing it all with schoolwork has taken perseverance."Never give up... pray to God. Listen to your parents, education is first, that's all," says Sierra. She and 11-year-old Josephine are still on a high, after their World Cup appearance midway through the game that saw Spain beat Argentina at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey."I saw Messi and Lamine Yamal!" says Josephine about the two team's stars - Argentinian captain Lionel Messi and Spain's teenage winger Yamal."I was so happy to see Messi and people watching us. I felt so excited and I was smiling, and a little bit nervous," she recalls."Shakira, she's very kind," chimes in Sierra.Figure caption, Stars shine at half-time showThe children gave Colombian pop star Shakira and Nigerian musician Burna Boy a big hug on stage as their performance ended - a moment their manager, Dauda Kavuma, insists was a natural show of affection, rather than clever choreography.Learning they had been picked to perform was a dream come true. The children "ran around in a circle, banging and shouting" when they learned the news, says Kavuma."They had already danced to Waka Waka, external in Britain's Got Talent," he explains about Shakira's remake of the 1980s Cameroonian classic Zangaléwa by Golden Sounds, external."But it was now a great moment to see that Shakira invited us... to perform with her."It means a lot and it's life-changing."Kavuma's philosophy is that there is so much talent in the ghetto, you just have to polish it.As a child he lived on the streets of Uganda's capital before the kindness of a teacher changed his life.He wanted to give back and later became a teacher himself before creating the Ghetto Kids dance troupe - formed of homeless children and those who could not afford school fees. Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Frequent practice is a part of life for the Ghetto Kids, who have a huge social media followingCombining a multitude of African dance styles, comedy and pure joy, they soon caught the attention of Ugandan musicians including Eddy Kenzo, who asked them to feature in some of his videos.The group's strategy has involved harnessing the viral-making powers of the internet, and their biggest break followed in 2017 when they appeared in the music video for French Montana's song Unforgettable - which at the time of writing has amassed more than 1.9 billion views on YouTube, external. That recognition opened yet more doors, leading the Ghetto Kids to the final of Britain's Got Talent in 2023, before also competing in America's Got Talent the following year. It has also enabled Kavuma to expand his project offering housing, food and tuition to many children across Uganda.This year's football World Cup final may have been the Ghetto Kids' biggest stage yet, but it was not their first major sporting event.Back in 2023, the Ghetto Kids were thrilled to meet Kylian Mbappé and perform at a football half-time match in France between rivals Paris Saint-Germain and Reims.Another recent career highlight was a film being made about their story, called Ghetto Kids Documentary: No Plan B.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, "Education first" is the message their parents and manager have drilled into the young dancersDespite their fame, the children's parents and manager have instilled in them an "education-first" mentality.Videos for their vast social media following are filmed at weekends, so that weekdays are largely kept free for school, Kavuma says. If they have to travel for performances, the children connect online to their teachers while away and catch up on any missed work once back in Kampala.Both Sierra and Josephine tell the BBC they plan to become doctors when they grow up but will never give up their passion for dance."Dancing changed my life - I went to school because of dance," says Sierra.Josephine agrees: "Dance is what I know and that makes me happy because that's my talent."So, what do they want to say to other children who, like them, might be talented but have not had the easiest start in life?"To love themselves, believe in God, and pray. Be with their talents - don't deny them," answers Josephine."And we love them."Image source, Getty Images for Global CitizenImage caption, Big hugs from Burna Boy and Shakira at the half-time showYou may also be interested in:

schema.headline: Uganda's Ghetto Kids: Dancing with Shakira and Burna Boy at the World Cup 'very, very, very, very, very good'

title: Jurgen Klopp: Germany boss threatens to quit new job if media invade family's privacy
description: Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.The former Liverpool manager w
body: Jurgen Klopp started his reign as Germany's head coach by threatening to quit if the media invades his family's privacy.The former Liverpool manager was appointed on a four-year deal on Friday to replace Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned this month after Germany's shock World Cup defeat by Paraguay in the last 32.But the 59-year-old issued a warning to the media as he held his first news conference as Germany's head coach."If you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace then I'll be gone, I'll just turn away," Klopp said."I know there are other countries where national team coaches are treated even worse."I'm not doing this job for myself, I'm doing it for you. I'm taking this job even though I've seen how you've treated Julian Nagelsmann and Thomas Tuchel."I love this job but I am always ready to call it quits if need be."Both Nagelsmann and England boss Tuchel came under media scrutiny after their exits from the World Cup, with Tuchel criticised for his defensive tactics and substitutions as the Three Lions let slip a 1-0 lead in their semi-final defeat by Argentina.Klopp's appointment was widely expected for weeks and his contract will see him through to the 2030 World Cup, co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco."Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any 'career' after the national team," he added. "This is the pinnacle, the absolutely high point of my footballing career as coach. I will give everything I have got."

schema.headline: Jurgen Klopp: Germany boss threatens to quit new job if media invade family's privacy

title: Why Jimothy the raccoon has become a mega meme online
description: How Jimothy the raccoon became the internet's latest animal obsessionImage source, Instagram/Kiana HallByLiv McMahon and Laura CressTechnology reporte
body: How Jimothy the raccoon became the internet's latest animal obsessionImage source, Instagram/Kiana HallByLiv McMahon and Laura CressTechnology reportersUpdated 6 hours agoCharli XCX might be hoping the release of her new album sets off another Brat summer, but many believe the season has already been claimed by a furrier force - Jimothy.First spotted bounding across streets in Washington, the Seattle raccoon with an unusual, spindly shape and the scamper of a Tasmanian Devil has been seized on by the internet as a new hit meme.Like Moo Deng and Neil the Seal before him, he is the latest cute, distinctive and seemingly chaotic creature to be immortalised in amateur footage, sometimes cringeworthy brand posts, and even murals.But what is it about Jimothy, as he's been nicknamed, that has gripped the internet?This Instagram post cannot be displayed in your browser. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.It all began with an innocuous video shared by Seattle resident Kiana Hall on Instagram."What am I looking at?" Hall could be heard exclaiming, as the unusual-looking raccoon hurtles across a pavement and up some nearby steps.A caption alongside it referred to the creature as "Jimothy the raccoon with short spine syndrome".While it is not known for sure if the condition has caused his appearance, many have assumed as such, and the description has stuck.As Hall's Instagram reel spread, it attracted more and more likes, comments and reposts, with more than eight million views as of Friday morning."My brother was talking about Jimothy the other day, and I asked him who he is," reads one comment on Hall's video. "He told me Jimothy would find me, and now he has."Some users have also praised the raccoon's online fame for drawing attention to spine conditions."I hope that someone can care for Jimothy as a wild animal... he will get older and need more care," wrote one user, who said she had been born with a congenital spine syndrome.Jimothy would not be the first to attract online fame for such a condition, Australian YouTuber Lessons in Meme Culture points out, external.A dog called Pig became a brief internet sensation in 2014 owing in part to having short spine syndrome.Why is he everywhere?In a strange pop cultural tradition that covers the likes of Doge and Grumpy Cat, Jimothy has found himself in the crosshairs of media attention for being two things - an unusual animal and very shareable."As cities expand and food waste increases, humans and raccoons cross paths more often," said Dr Idil Galip, digital culture researcher at the University of Amsterdam."More encounters mean more footage of raccoons being funny and in today's fast-moving, saturated feeds, that footage can become a meme almost instantly."He hasn't just been celebrated in posts from fans across social media.The online outpouring of love for Jimothy has also since translated into the real world - with one local artist celebrating him with a mural in the neighbourhood of Ballard, where he was first spotted.This Instagram post cannot be displayed in your browser. Please enable Javascript or try a different browser.View original content on InstagramThe BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.Skip instagram post 2Allow Instagram content?This article contains content provided by Instagram.  We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies.  You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites.President Donald Trump's White House social media accounts, no stranger to tapping into online culture to promote his agenda, have also shared a Jimothy meme.In a post on X, external, it portrayed the raccoon donning a red hat emblazoned with "Trump was right about everything".Blissfully unaware of his 15 seconds of viral fame, the raccoon has become fodder for brands racing to capitalise on consumer interest in the latest online trend.Among the things Jimothy has amassed so far are:A Google animation which runs across the screen when you search "Jimothy"Meme coins named in his honour - part of a grand tradition where crypto fans jump on viral moments to make digital coins with questionable valueAn upcoming appearance, external in World of Warcraft's fictional Azeroth"Meme marketing is now standard practice for many brands," said Dr Galip."They will hop on to whatever's trending, hoping the visibility rubs off on them. "A viral moment can give momentary brand visibility, in searches and social media feeds, where the attention is."He's even popped up in Minecraft, or so the official account claims.From naughty penguins to ungovernable elephant seals, funny animals attracting attention on the internet is nothing new.But the surge of interest and drive to document these quirky, characterful creatures can often result in pleas from local officials to respect their privacy and safety.People in Washington and its most populous city Seattle have been similarly warned not to approach Jimothy to protect him and themselves."As long as you don't try to pet him, cuddle him or feed him, Jimothy poses zero public health risk," said the state health department on Threads, external.Figure caption, But in an otherwise overwhelming online landscape, some feel these viral moments offer some relief."The internet is a lot. It is too much, constantly, in every direction," writes Jamie Slack on her blog, Totally the Bomb, external."And then Jimothy shows up and for one brief weird moment everyone is on the same page - rooting for this little gremlin, giggling at his name, feeling weirdly connected to strangers over absolutely nothing."

title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
description: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.She told BBC Breakfast tha
body: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment."Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market."We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England. Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing"."There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents. "We need rent controls, and we need them now."Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters". "Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time. Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property. The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".Rayner was also asked about the government's target of building 1.5 million new homes by the end of the parliament in 2029.She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the target had become more challenging to meet, pointing to increased construction costs as one of the reasons for that. "1.5 million homes is a difficult target. It was when I made the target, but I'm going to keep the target, and I'm not going to be defeated," she said.The Tories say the target is a "dead letter because of her party's taxes and red tape".During Burnham's bid to replace Sir Keir Starmer as Labour leader and prime minister, he promised to deliver the biggest programme of council house building in decades. He has also long talked about implementing reforms to property taxes, including stamp duty and council tax - though he has not specified what exactly he would change while in government.Burnham has pledged to lead a "cost of living government" and has announced a series of measures in his first week in office which he said were designed to give people "breathing space". The measures include cutting VAT on household energy bills from October and restoring a £2 bus fare cap in England, except London, from January 2027.

schema.headline: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England

title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton leads Charles Leclerc in Ferrari one-two in Friday practice
description: With a new Honda engine due for the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after Formula 1's summer break, Alonso said there was a "positive atmosphere in th
body: With a new Honda engine due for the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after Formula 1's summer break, Alonso said there was a "positive atmosphere in the team now"."The car feels more glued to the ground and easier to drive to an extent when you are in control of the grip in the corners," Alonso added."More predictable and an easier car but still a long way to go for us."Obviously this will be the first step. We need to find more performance both on the chassis but also on the engine."Zandvoort would be a good test for us with the new engine. So step by step but definitely in the right direction."The key was not only that the upgrade was a step in the right direction but also that it had delivered as expected.There had been some nervousness around that for the first major upgrade under Adrian Newey's technical leadership. In the past three seasons, upgrades had not delivered as expected, and it was critical for the future that this one, designed and developed with new tools at the team's new factory, worked.Newey said further upgrades to the car were due for the Italian and Azerbaijan Grands Prix in September.Alonso said: "We had what we expected in terms of numbers and correlation, which is obviously very encouraging for the future as well, for next year's car and the future upgrades into this year."It's still a long way to go for us. Obviously, we're starting so far behind, but this is the first step, hopefully, of good ones coming."The day was not all positive for Aston Martin, however. Alonso's team-mate Lance Stroll spun out of the first session with what initially appeared to be a rear suspension failure.He was then unable to take part in the second because there was not enough time to repair the car.Team representative Pedro de la Rosa said: "It is a suspension failure. We were confident it would not happen in Fernando's car. That's why we sent him out. Because of the lack of spares we couldn't repair his car on time. Some parts need to be repaired and some needed to come here."Ferrari had been expected to be strong at this track, which is one of the least power-dependent on the calendar, as it has the best car in the corners but it is lacking engine performance.But Leclerc was cautious about reading too much into it. Hamilton did not speak to the media - only one driver from each team does a pooled interview on Fridays."It was a relatively strong day," Leclerc said. "I felt good with the car and the performance seemed to be there straight away so that's a good thing but the weekend is long."From the Friday to Saturday we see teams making a jump in performance. Normally we are on the back foot on Friday so it's a good thing we have a good Friday but we still need to stay on it and work hard to get better tomorrow."It is going to be tight tomorrow. I don't expect us to have the gap we have today, we will have to do everything perfect. But if the feeling is there I am sure we will do a good job in Q3."George Russell was 0.933secs off the pace and behind Norris, with a significant upgrade on the McLaren, and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.The Briton said: "It's a bit of a shame because Budapest is one of the most enjoyable circuits to drive. They have resurfaced a third of the track and they've done a really bad job. It's really bumpy."The track is braking up in the last corner so people are driving around the middle of the last corner and not hitting the apex. "The underlying car pace doesn't seem as competitive as we saw in Silverstone and Spa. There is a lot of room to improve. The wind is shifting a lot and that has a real impact into car balance. Hopefully tomorrow will be better."Antonelli, leading Hamilton by 45 points and Russell by 50, did not complete a qualifying simulation lap in the second session.His first had to be abandoned when Franco Colapinto crashed his Alpine at the last corner, and his second came to grief when he made an error going into the chicane.Antonelli was complaining all session about rear brake locking, but he was on a par with Norris' time in the first sector on both laps before they were curtailed.Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "Lack of grip and balance, both drivers had to wind some front wing out, but on the long runs looked pretty consistent and competitive compared to the Ferrari, Red Bull and McLarens."Behind Russell, Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was sixth fastest, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and McLaren's Oscar Piastri.Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.Friday practice results

title: ICC top prosecutor removed over sexual misconduct allegations
description: Members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have voted to dismiss Karim Khan as chief prosecutor for alleged sexual misconduct.Elected the ICC's
body: Members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have voted to dismiss Karim Khan as chief prosecutor for alleged sexual misconduct.Elected the ICC's third prosecutor in 2021, Khan was suspended last month. The decision to remove him was passed with 82 votes in favour.The court's oversight body found in June he had committed a "serious breach of duty and serious misconduct" by engaging in an improper sexual relationship with a junior ICC staff member and seeking to stop her pursuing her complaint.Khan has repeatedly denied all the allegations against him. His lawyer said he would challenge "the lawfulness and fairness of the decision through all available legal mechanisms".It was not immediately clear what legal avenues remained open to the ousted prosecutor.The entire process, however, goes beyond the fate of a single prosecutor and could reshape the world's only permanent war‑crimes tribunal.The misconduct investigation has put the institution under a glaring spotlight, intensified divisions inside it and played out alongside an unprecedented campaign to weaken, and in fact dismantle, the ICC in its entirety.The fear among its supporters is that the court will emerge weakened and less able to face the gravest global threats.Khan, a prominent British lawyer, has been on voluntary leave to fight the allegations since May 2025. He remains suspended from practising law in the UK, after the Bar Standards Board imposed an interim ban while it conducts its own inquiry.He was unable to attend the vote, held in the United Nations headquarters in New York, because he is barred from entering the United States under sanctions imposed by the Trump administration over the ICC's investigation into alleged war crimes by Israeli officials in Gaza.Regardless of his removal, the controversy is unlikely to end there.The decision follows a highly sensitive process that has left the court under intense scrutiny.In May 2024, allegations that Khan had engaged in sexual misconduct involving a female staff member were reported to the ICC by a third party.The court's Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) opened an investigation, but the case was later closed after the alleged victim declined to participate.Critics of the process argued that the investigation had been mishandled, undermining confidence in the IOM.Investigators ultimately said there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the allegations.A second referral was made in October 2024. The matter was then transferred to the United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), which conducted a broader investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of authority.That inquiry ran from November 2024 to December 2025 and generated more than 5,000 pages of evidence and testimony.The OIOS findings were subsequently reviewed by a panel of three judges tasked with advising whether Khan's conduct amounted to serious misconduct, less serious misconduct, or no misconduct.The allegations have unfolded during a period of exceptional pressure on the ICC,  coinciding with wider political tensions.The United States imposed sanctions on Khan after he sought arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes linked to the war in Gaza.Washington's attitude to the court in general has become increasingly hostile in recent years.Earlier this month, the US launched a new "whole‑of‑government" campaign to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" in what it calls a threat to American sovereignty, promising visa bans, asset freezes and diplomatic pressure on allies to withdraw from the court or reject its jurisdiction over their nationals.The United States, Russia and Israel are not members of the ICC. However, the court can exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed by their nationals on the territory of ICC member states.

schema.headline: ICC top prosecutor removed over sexual misconduct allegations
